notes.meaning: God speaks to Cyrus, the Persian king, long before Cyrus did his great work. He calls Cyrus His "anointed," which means someone set apart and equipped for a special job. No oil was poured on him. God holds his hand to strengthen and guide him, takes strength away from other kings, and opens city gates before him. The old writers note that on the night Babylon fell, the gates by the river were left open, and Cyrus's army marched in.

God promises to go ahead of Cyrus and clear every obstacle out of his way. "Level the mountains" is a picture of a smooth road. Babylon was famous for its great gates of bronze, so breaking bronze gates and iron bars means no defense will be able to stop him.

The "treasures of darkness" are riches hidden away in vaults or buried underground. Cyrus did gain huge wealth when he conquered rich cities like Sardis and Babylon. God gives him these riches so that Cyrus will know that Israel's God is the true LORD. Ezra 1 shows that Cyrus did honor God for his success. Still, Calvin notes that Cyrus never truly turned to worship God alone.

God explains why He blesses Cyrus. It is for the sake of His people Israel, whom He chose. It is not because Cyrus deserves it. God called Cyrus by name and gave him a title of honor even though Cyrus did not know Him. Even when kingdoms rise and fall, God is working for the good of His people.

God says it plainly: He alone is God, and there is no other. "I will equip you" (older Bibles say "gird") means God gives Cyrus strength and power. It is the opposite of verse 1, where God takes strength away from other kings. Cyrus's own idols did not make him strong. The God he did not know did.

"From where the sun rises to where it sets" means from east to west, the whole world. God wants all people to learn through these events that He alone is God. His long-ago promises and Cyrus's amazing success would spread His fame among the nations.

God is in charge of everything, the good times and the hard times. "Calamity" (older Bibles say "evil") here means trouble, war, or disaster. It does not mean sin. God is not the author of sin, but He rules over suffering and judgment. Many writers also think God is answering the Persian belief in two rival gods, one good and one evil. There is only one God, and He rules over both light and darkness.

differ.view: God is the author of all events, good and bad. He does not put malice in wicked people, but He uses their malice to discipline His people, as He did with Pharaoh.
Evil came into the world through sin, which God did not want. God gave people real freedom to choose.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: God can never do moral evil. This verse speaks of natural evils, like hardship, which God can use for good purposes.

notes.meaning: God commands the sky and the ground to work together, like rain making crops grow. What grows is righteousness, meaning right living and God's faithfulness, together with salvation. The first meaning is Israel's rescue from Babylon. The old writers also see a picture of Christ's salvation and the pouring out of the Holy Spirit. Salvation and righteousness grow together, so we should not expect one without the other.

Arguing with God is as silly as a clay pot complaining to the potter. Some of God's people grumbled about their long exile, or about God using a foreign king to save them. We are fragile "pots" like everyone else. We have no right to tell our Maker He is doing it wrong. Paul uses the same picture in Romans 9.

A child who scolds his parents for bringing him into the world would be shocking and rude. Complaining against God for how He runs our lives is even worse. If God is our Father, we owe Him trust and respect.

God names Himself the Holy One and Maker of Israel. In this translation He rebukes those who demand that He explain Himself, or who try to tell Him how to treat His own children. Older Bibles read "Ask me... command ye me," and some writers take that as a warm invitation. On that reading, we should not argue with God, but we may bring our needs to Him in humble, trusting prayer.

God made the earth, the people on it, the sky, and the stars. Because He made everything, He rules everything. If He cares for the whole world, He will surely take care of His own people. That is good news for anyone who feels small and helpless.

God has raised up Cyrus "in righteousness," meaning He did it to keep His promises to His people. Cyrus would order Jerusalem to be rebuilt and set the exiles free without asking any ransom. Captives were rarely freed that way, so it showed God was behind it. The old writers also see a picture of Christ, who sets people free from sin at no cost to them.

Faraway nations like Egypt and Cush will bring their wealth to God's people. They will come humbly and say, "God is truly with you, and there is no other God." Some of this came true when Persia helped pay for rebuilding the temple. The writers say it came true more fully when people from every nation came to faith in Christ and joined His church. The "chains" are seen as a bond these nations choose for themselves.

The prophet is amazed at God's ways. During the exile God seemed hidden and silent, yet He was quietly working all along to save His people. His plans are often too deep for us to see. Even when we cannot see what He is doing, He is still Israel's God and Savior, so we can wait for Him patiently.
People who make and trust idols will end up ashamed. When they need help, their idols will fail them. Even if they stand together and cheer each other on, they will all be let down together.

Idol-worshippers are put to shame, but those who trust the LORD never will be. God promises Israel a salvation that lasts forever. The writers see this pointing beyond the return from Babylon to eternal salvation of the soul through the Messiah.

God made the earth with a purpose. He did not make it to sit empty, but to be a home for people. This also meant that the land of Judah, left empty during the exile, would be filled with people again. The God who made the world and keeps it going is the only true God.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some people use this verse to support the "gap theory." That is the idea of a long stretch of time between Genesis 1:1 and 1:2, since God says He did not create the earth empty.

notes.meaning: Pagan oracles (places where people asked gods about the future) often gave murky answers from dark caves. God is different. He has spoken openly and clearly. He never told His people to seek Him for nothing, and He keeps His word. Jesus said something similar about His own teaching: "I have spoken nothing in secret" (John 18:20).

God calls together the people of the nations who survived the wars of those days. He tells them plainly that carrying a wooden idol and praying to it is foolish, because it cannot save anyone. God wants even the nations to be cured of trusting idols.

God dares idol-worshippers to make their best case. Which god told about these events long before they happened? Only the LORD did. He is both a righteous God and a Savior. His fairness and His saving love go together, and that is why we can trust Him.

Here is a wide-open invitation to the whole world: turn to God and be saved. Older Bibles say "look unto me." Like the Israelites who looked at the bronze serpent and lived, we are saved by looking to God in faith, not by our own efforts. The famous preacher Charles Spurgeon came to faith through this verse when a lay preacher told him, "Look to Christ."

God makes a solemn promise, swearing by Himself because there is no one greater. One day every knee will bow to Him, and every tongue will pledge loyalty to Him. Paul applies this to Jesus (Romans 14:11; Philippians 2:10). It begins as the gospel spreads and will be complete when Christ judges the world. Worship belongs both in the heart and in what we openly say.

People will say that only in the LORD do we find righteousness and strength. Righteousness here means being made right with God, and strength means power to live for Him. Believers admit they have neither in themselves and receive both from God. People will come to Him, and some former enemies will turn to Him in sorrow. Those who keep fighting against Him will end in shame.

All of God's true people will be "justified" in the LORD, which means declared right with Him. Then they will rejoice and boast in Him. The old writers say this "Israel" includes believing Jews and also believers from every nation. We are made right through Christ, not by our own good deeds, so our only boast is in the Lord.
